reader_situation: A homeowner hears popping, rumbling, crackling, or another new sound from a tank water heater and wants to know whether it is dangerous, whether they can fix it with a flush, and when the heater is due for replacement.
direct_answer: Popping and rumbling usually mean sediment on the bottom of the tank is trapping steam bubbles; A.O. Smith's fix is a flush, and it recommends flushing at least once a year (more often in hard water). Different sounds point elsewhere: crackling can be aluminum-anode gel, screeching a blower or electric element, humming loose parts, banging water hammer. A leaking T&P valve, a leak at the base, or a heater over 10 years old changes the answer.
consensus: Popping or rumbling is caused by sediment at the bottom of the tank
Flush a tank water heater about once a year
Sediment lowers efficiency and can shorten the heater's life
Turn off power or gas and let the water cool before draining
Tank water heaters last roughly a decade
gaps: Each noise has a different cause in A.O. Smith's guide: popping = sediment trapping steam bubbles; crackling = sediment or aluminum hydroxide gel beads from an aluminum anode reacting with chlorine (consider an aluminum-zinc anode); screeching/whistling = dirty blower wheel or blocked vent on blower units, a failing blower motor, or a bad element on electric units; humming = loose components; banging = water slamming into shutoff valves (water hammer arrestor).

Hard water needs more frequent flushing; USGS classifies hardness as 0-60 mg/L soft, 61-120 moderately hard, 121-180 hard, over 180 very hard, and says hard water forms calcium carbonate deposits when heated that raise heating costs and reduce electric water heater efficiency.

Anode inspection is yearly in A.O. Smith's maintenance guide, not every 3-5 years: a healthy rod is smooth and about half an inch in diameter; replace it if it shows deterioration or several inches of exposed core wire. A.O. Smith's noise page says an anode usually lasts about 5 years.

T&P valve: lift the lever yearly to confirm water discharges, and have a professional inspect it every 5 years (A.O. Smith); if no water releases, replace the valve; a leaking T&P valve may indicate an unsafe temperature or pressure situation.

Thermal expansion: water expands as it heats and raises tank pressure; A.O. Smith generally recommends an expansion tank and Bradford White says never to operate a heater in a closed system without thermal-expansion control.
Gas heaters can form condensation when cold water enters the tank or when the burner fires after sitting idle; A.O. Smith says this is typically temporary.

Flush logistics: draining takes 20-40 minutes (A.O. Smith); if sediment clogs the drain valve, call a plumber; after closing the drain, run a hot faucet at least 3 minutes to purge air. Refill fully before restoring power (registry).

Repair vs. replace: A.O. Smith gives 8-12 years average life and says a heater over 10 years old that leaks around the base or operates erratically is probably due for replacement; a corroded or cracked tank means replacement. Bradford White says its heaters can last 10 years or more with professional installation and maintenance, and advises calling a plumbing professional for any sound outside normal operation.

evidence.detail: Popping: sediment at the bottom traps steam bubbles; flush the tank. Crackling: sediment or aluminum hydroxide (jelly-like green, blue, or gray beads) from an aluminum anode reacting with excess chlorine; flush and consider an aluminum-zinc anode. Screeching/whistling: dirty blower wheel or blocked vent; failed blower motor bearings; bad heating element on electric heaters. Humming: loose components vibrating; on ultra-low NOx gas heaters may indicate a damaged burner. Banging: water slamming into internal shutoff valves; install a water hammer arrestor.
evidence.source_title: Water Heater Making Noise | A. O. Smith

evidence.claim: Flush frequency and anode life (noise page)
evidence.detail: Flush at least once a year, more often with hard water, older pipes, or heavy buildup. Anode rod usually lasts about 5 years and could dissipate sooner depending on water.
evidence.source_title: Water Heater Making Noise | A. O. Smith

evidence.detail: Turn the heater off for a few hours before draining; shut the cold supply; attach a hose; open a hot faucet to prevent pressure building; open the drain. Most water heaters take 20 to 40 minutes to drain completely. If sediment clogs the drain valve, call a plumber or service technician. Flush with cold water until sediment stops; close the drain when water runs clear; run the hot faucet at least 3 minutes to remove trapped air. Most water heaters should be flushed at least once a year; more often in hard water areas.
evidence.source_title: How To Drain (Flush) a Water Heater | A. O. Smith

evidence.detail: Inspect the anode rod once a year; a rod in good condition is smooth and around a half inch in diameter; replace it if it shows deterioration or several inches of exposed core wire. The T&P valve should be inspected once a year by the consumer and every 5 years by a professional: lift the lever to open and close a few times to make sure water discharges. Temperature typically no higher than 120 F. Sediment reduces efficiency and can clog water lines.
evidence.source_title: How to Maintain a Water Heater | A. O. Smith

evidence.detail: Strange noises typically mean sediment buildup (rumbling, popping, banging, hissing or sizzling). Flush at least once a year to rid it of sediment that causes failure. Average life expectancy about 8 to 12 years. If the heater is more than 10 years old, leaks around the base of the tank, or operates erratically, replacement is probably right. Test the pressure relief valve by lifting the handle; if it does not release water, install a new valve.
evidence.source_title: When to Repair or Replace a Water Heater | A. O. Smith

evidence.detail: Water expands during heating, creating higher pressure in the tank; A.O. Smith generally recommends an expansion tank. In extreme cases the T&P valve may open to release excess pressure and hot water. A leaking T&P valve may indicate an unsafe temperature or pressure situation.
evidence.source_title: Tank Water Heaters and Safety | A. O. Smith

evidence.detail: Gas heaters may experience condensation when cold water enters the tank and when the burner fires after a period of inactivity; typically temporary and not a cause for concern. Leaks from the side often originate from the T&P relief valve, often caused by excessive temperature or pressure. A corroded or cracked tank typically means replacing the water heater.
evidence.source_title: Why Is My Water Heater Leaking? | A. O. Smith

evidence.detail: Sediment buildup creates an insulating barrier between the heating source and the water, so the unit must work harder and longer to produce hot water; many water heater failures and efficiency issues trace back to sediment accumulation; sand and rust particles contribute to sediment.
evidence.source_title: How Sediment Buildup Affects Your Water Heater Efficiency | Bradford White

evidence.claim: Manufacturer guidance on noises, draining, expansion, lifespan
evidence.detail: If your water heater is making a sound outside of normal operation, contact a plumbing professional. Water heaters are not self-cleaning; periodic draining is still needed. Do not operate the water heater in a closed system without provisions for controlling thermal expansion. A rotten egg smell requires a plumbing professional. With professional installation and proper maintenance, heaters can last 10 years or more.

Hardness is dissolved calcium and magnesium. 0-60 mg/L as calcium carbonate is soft, 61-120 moderately hard, 121-180 hard, more than 180 very hard. Heated hard water forms solid calcium carbonate deposits that can shorten equipment life, raise heating costs, and reduce electric water heater efficiency.
evidence.source_title: Hardness of Water | U.S. Geological Survey

original_asset.spec: Sound-by-sound table (popping, crackling, screeching/whistling, humming, banging, water at the T&P valve) with cause, first step, and when a pro is needed, from A.O. Smith and Bradford White; plus a yearly maintenance schedule (flush yearly or more in hard water by USGS category, anode inspection yearly with replacement criteria, T&P lift test yearly and pro inspection every 5 years) and an age-based repair/replace rule (over 10 years plus leaks at the base).

cautions: Registry flush order: power/gas off, cool, close cold inlet, drain, flush, close drain, refill fully until a hot tap runs air-free, only then restore power. An electric element fired dry burns out.
Hot water scalds: let the tank cool; keep clear of the T&P discharge pipe when lift-testing.
Gas work beyond basic relighting, rotten-egg smell in the water, a leaking tank, or a T&P valve that discharges on its own go to a professional.
Do not invent a plumber cost range or an efficiency percentage; no fetched source gives one.
